title: Making Up and Resolving a Problem Are Not the Same
deck: Restoring closeness can matter, but a problem only begins to be resolved when the actual arrangements change.
body: After an argument ends, two people start talking again, eat together, and can even joke as usual.
The tension is gone, and warmth has returned to the relationship. Naturally, they feel the matter has been resolved.
But making up and resolving a problem are not the same thing.
Making up concerns whether the two can draw close again now. Resolving a problem requires examining whether the conditions that caused the conflict have changed.
The two can happen together or be entirely separate.
Some conflicts really are only misunderstandings. Once the facts are clear and the two people understand each other again, the problem disappears as closeness returns.
Other conflicts arise from longstanding arrangements.

Who always makes the decisions? Who bears more of the consequences? Whose refusal is continually reinterpreted? Whose reasons are heard only when they do not change the status quo? These things do not change automatically because both people become gentle again.
Warmth has returned, but their original positions remain.
It is easy to mistake making up for resolution because conflict itself is painful.

Silence, distance, and uncertainty make both people anxious. Drawing close again immediately eases that pain. By comparison, rearranging responsibilities, changing habits, or acknowledging that a shared plan no longer fits is much harder.
So the relationship opts to restore the feeling first.
There is nothing wrong with this. People may only be able to keep discussing difficulties once they feel safe enough. The question is whether a short rest is treated as closing the case for good.
“Haven’t we already made up? Why bring it up again?”
This treats renewed closeness as grounds for no further discussion.

The person raising the old problem then seems to be disrupting the peace. If they go on, they are held responsible for fresh unpleasantness; if they stop, the original problem simply waits to reappear.
Over time, making up can become a cycle.
Conflict arises, and both withdraw; after pain accumulates, one gives way first; closeness returns, and the problem is shelved; the same pattern appears again.
Every reconciliation is real, and every time the problem remains.
Genuine resolution is usually quieter than making up.

It need not involve intense emotion, but leaves changes in the life that follows. Matters once decided by one person become subjects of real negotiation; a refusal no longer undergoes repeated scrutiny; burdens are redistributed; an apology goes beyond words and changes subsequent actions.
Resolving a problem does not require identical accounts of the past.

Both may still feel their own pain was greater, and may retain different understandings of motives. What matters is whether they jointly recognize a fact that must change and each take responsibility for the part they can carry out.
Making up cannot replace this change, and change need not come with a guarantee of making up.

Sometimes, once a problem is finally clear, both discover the relationship cannot continue. They cannot jointly commit to a certain direction, or cannot both accommodate a certain boundary. The matter is resolved, but the relationship ends.
This sounds contradictory because we are used to understanding “resolution” as staying.
But parting honestly sometimes comes closer to resolution than repeatedly restoring closeness. At least neither is using brief warmth to sustain an arrangement that cannot work.
Conversely, a relationship may continue before its problems are fully resolved.
People fall back into old patterns and need time. Both can say: “We can’t do it yet, but we know where the problem is and agree on how to handle it next time.”
This unfinished work differs from pretending the work is finished.
The former acknowledges that action is still needed; the latter only asks that the matter no longer be raised.
So, after making up, it may help to ask an unromantic question:
Apart from feeling close again, what has actually changed?
If the answer is nothing, that does not immediately negate the value of making up. Restoring connection may matter in itself.
But it should make further resolution possible, rather than serve as a reason to escape it.
A good relationship can do more than embrace again after conflict.
After the embrace, it can return to the table that has not yet been cleared and keep discussing what brings both people back to the same place, again and again.
entry_door: This essay uses no theoretical terms, but behind it lies the same question: how can a relationship draw close to someone without living their life for them? To follow this line of thought further, start with Non Dubito in Five Minutes.
